elements.id-string-9: In recent years, language models (LMs), such as GPT-4, have been widely used in multiple domains, including natural language processing, visualization, and so on.
elements.id-string-10: However, applying them for analyzing and optimizing high-performance computing (HPC) software is still challenging due to the lack of HPC-specific support.
elements.id-string-11: In this paper, we design the \ourwork framework to facilitate the research and development of HPC software analyses and optimizations using LMs.
elements.id-string-12: Tailored for supporting HPC datasets, AI models, and pipelines, our framework is built on top of a range of components from different levels of the machine learning software stack, with \face-compatible APIs.
elements.id-string-13: Using three representative tasks, we evaluated the prototype of our framework.
elements.id-string-14: The results show that \ourwork can help users quickly evaluate a set of state-of-the-art models and generate insightful leaderboards.\keywords{Language model  \and Programming language processing \and High-performance computing}
elements.id-string-16: Language models (LMs) are models designed to understand and generate human language.
elements.id-string-17: In recent years, large language models (LLMs)
elements.id-string-18: trained on large amounts of text data have demonstrated stunning capabilities in various natural language processing and visualization tasks.
elements.id-string-19: They have also been widely used to process programming languages due to the similarities between natural languages and programming languages.
elements.id-string-20: For example, GPT-4~\cite{bubeck2023sparks} shows early signs of artificial general intelligence.
elements.id-string-21: Based on a large language model trained on code~\cite{chen2021evaluating}, GitHub provides an AI assistant for developing software.
elements.id-string-22: Given the rise of LLMs, it is natural for researchers and developers in the high-performance computing community to start exploiting LMs for addressing various challenges in HPC, including code analysis, code generation, performance optimization, question answering, and so on.
elements.id-string-23: However, mainstream frameworks of LMs were originally designed to serve natural language processing.
elements.id-string-24: It is difficult for newcomers in HPC to quickly access HPC-specific datasets, models, and pipelines.
elements.id-string-25: For example, the current popular \face platform does not include dedicated pipelines for software analyses and optimizations.
elements.id-string-26: Another challenge is the entire field is evolving quickly, with new techniques emerging almost weekly, making it challenging for HPC users to keep up with the latest techniques and find relevant ones.
elements.id-string-27: Last but not least, there is a lack of standard, reproducible evaluation processes for LMs focusing on HPC-specific tasks.
elements.id-string-28: Therefore, it is difficult to have a fair comparison among different models for a given HPC task.
elements.id-string-29: In this paper, we propose a framework (named \ourwork) designed to serve HPC users as first-class citizens by including internal components and external APIs relevant to HPC-specific tasks.
elements.id-string-30: \ourwork's components include models, datasets, pipelines, and so on, while the APIs allow users to interact with these components to finish given HPC tasks.
elements.id-string-31: We highlight the contributions of our work as follows:
elements.id-string-33: We design an extensible framework for including and exposing relevant machine learning components to facilitate the adoption of large language models for HPC-specific tasks.The framework provides a set of APIs to facilitate essential operations, including code preprocessing, tokenization, integration with new data, and evaluation.A set of pipelines have been developed to support common HPC tasks, including code similarity analysis, parallelism detection, question answering, and so on.We provide HPC-specific datasets such as DRB-ML, \crawldata, and OMPQA to support various HPC pipelines.Our work introduces standardized workflows and metrics to enable fair and reproducible evaluation of LLMs for HPC-specific tasks.Using three representative tasks, we demonstrated how the framework can be used to test a set of language models and generate leaderboards.
elements.id-string-35: Language models (LMs) are machine learning models designed to comprehend and generate human language.
elements.id-string-36: They can be used to facilitate natural and intuitive interactions between humans and machines.
elements.id-string-37: Early generations of LMs, using recurrent neural networks (RNNs),  showed inspiring results for various natural language processing (NLP) tasks.
elements.id-string-38: A transformative evolution by the Transformer \cite{vaswani2017attention} reveals remarkable potentials of LMs.
elements.id-string-40: models utilize the attention mechanism to capture the dependencies between all words in an input sentence, irrespective of their positions.
elements.id-string-41: Compared to RNNs, transformers process data in parallel rather than sequentially and significantly improve the efficiency of model training and inference.
elements.id-string-42: Transformers further enables the inauguration of the large language models (LLMs).
elements.id-string-43: Compared to LMs, LLMs are trained on a vast amount of data and possess parameter counts on the order of billions or more, allowing them to generate more detailed and nuanced responses.
elements.id-string-44: Examples of LLMs include OpenAI's GPT-3, GPT-4 and Google's BARD.
elements.id-string-45: Nowadays, LLMs have shown remarkable capabilities in NLP tasks like translation, question answering, and text generation.

elements.id-string-60: LMs are trained mainly by text data with a focus on NLP.
elements.id-string-61: The sources of the training data mainly come from books, web content, newspapers, scientific articles, and  other text data in various natural languages.
elements.id-string-62: Latest LLMs have demonstrated rich skill sets in NLP including text prediction, common sense reasoning, reading comprehension, translation and question answering.
elements.id-string-63: There has been a keen interest in deploying NLP techniques to programming language processing (PLP) tasks, such as code summarization, code generation, and code similarity analysis \cite{chen2022multi,flynn2022finding}.
elements.id-string-64: Previous studies have demonstrated successful applications of traditional language models to PLP tasks, showing the feasibility of this approach~\cite{devlin2018bert}.
elements.id-string-65: CodeBERT \cite{feng2020codebert}, for example, is a transformer-based model trained with a diverse range of programming languages and can be used for a variety of programming-related tasks.
elements.id-string-66: Similarly, CodeT5 \cite{wang2021codet5} is a variant of Google's T5 language model, trained specifically on code datasets to perform advanced programming tasks like code completion, bug detection, and code summarization.
elements.id-string-67: Lately, StarCoder \cite{li2023starcoder}, a 15B parameter model trained with 1 trillion tokens sourced from a large collection of permissively licensed GitHub repositories, is developed to be a Large Language Model mainly for code generation or completion.
elements.id-string-68: StarChat-Alpha is a GPT-like chat model fine-tuned from StarCoder to act as a helpful coding assistant.
elements.id-string-71: With the recent breakthroughs in Generative Pretrained Transformer (GPT) large language models \cite{brown2020language}, it has become increasingly intriguing to explore the application of large language models (LLMs) for HPC tasks.
elements.id-string-72: However, their deployment in the HPC domain is still relatively unexplored.
elements.id-string-73: This venture comes with various challenges, including:
elements.id-string-76: Pipelines: Traditional language model frameworks like Hugging Face were designed to support natural language processing or compute vision problems.
elements.id-string-77: Expanding LMs to any new domain, including HPC,  requires the addition of new pipelines designed to finish domain-specific tasks.Datasets: The HPC domain encompasses an extensive amount of code spanning various fields, including biology and climate modeling.
elements.id-string-78: However, preparing this data for machine learning training, such as labeling parallelizable loops in HPC programs for parallelism detection, presents significant challenges.
elements.id-string-79: The scarcity of ready-to-use, pre-labeled HPC datasets poses a particular obstacle for training language models, especially large ones, highlighting the need for more shared resources in the community.Pre-processing: Pre-processing in the context of LMs for HPC typically involves the conversion of source files into a sequence of tokens.
elements.id-string-80: However, the direct application of NLP tokenizers to code can be sub-optimal.
elements.id-string-81: For instance, an NLP tokenizer might split a variable name into two tokens, a scenario that is not desirable for PLP analysis.
elements.id-string-82: Also, models designed for processing source code may use graph representations, such as abstract syntax trees, to have better performance.Input size limit: Language models often have limited input token lengths (such as 512 to a few thousand of tokens).
elements.id-string-83: HPC tasks often involve processing large-scale software packages with millions of lines of source code.Evaluation: There is a pressing need for standardized and reproducible evaluation of different models in the context of various HPC tasks, using metrics suitable for domain-specific requirements.
elements.id-string-86: To address the challenges discussed in Section~\ref{sec-background}, we introduce \ourwork, a comprehensive framework that encapsulates a suite of machine learning components within user-friendly APIs.
elements.id-string-87: This framework is tailored for HPC users, simplifying the implementation process and making the robust capabilities of language models more accessible and user-friendly within the HPC community.
elements.id-string-88: The primary goal of \ourwork is to reduce the complexities inherent in employing language models, thus enabling HPC users to leverage their powerful capabilities more effectively and efficiently.
elements.id-string-90: Figure~\ref{fig:architecture} provides the overview of the \ourwork framework.
elements.id-string-91: It is built on top of multiple internal machine learning components with \face-compatible APIs.
elements.id-string-92: Higher-level components provide concepts and interfaces to users, while middle or lower-level components provide implementation support.

elements.id-string-100: HPC users are interested in a wide range of tasks related to programming language processing.
elements.id-string-101: Table~\ref{tab-HPC-tasks} outlines one way to categorize HPC-specific tasks.
elements.id-string-102: The purpose here is not to provide a comprehensive taxonomy of all tasks but a starting point for common tasks we are interested in supporting in our framework.
elements.id-string-103: Most tasks are self-explanatory by names and each may have further sub-tasks.
elements.id-string-104: For example, clone detection can be viewed as a specialized sub-task under code similarity analysis.

elements.id-string-107: In the context of machine learning, a pipeline represents a sequence of data processing stages to complete a task.
elements.id-string-108: Our \ourwork framework extends the pipeline function provided by \face, adapting it for HPC tasks.
elements.id-string-109: We have developed three inference pipelines: code similarity analysis, parallelism detection, and OpenMP question answering.
elements.id-string-110: Code similarity analysis determines the similarity between a pair of code snippets.
elements.id-string-111: Parallel detection is defined to check if an input code snippet can be parallelized or not using OpenMP.
elements.id-string-112: The OpenMP question answering pipeline is designed to use models to generate answers to OpenMP-related questions.
elements.id-string-113: Tokenizers are responsible for preprocessing input into an array of numbers as inputs to a model.
elements.id-string-114: They are essential components used by pipelines.
elements.id-string-115: Most LM tokenizers are primarily designed for NLP tasks.
elements.id-string-116: For instance, given a function name \texttt{my\_func}, a typical NLP tokenizer like BERT might split it into separate tokens (such as `\texttt{my}', `\texttt{\_}', and `\texttt{func}') while a code-aware tokenizer may treat the function name as a single entity to ensure a more meaningful representation.
elements.id-string-117: To overcome this, we developed the \ourwork tokenizer, leveraging the treesitter~\cite{treesitter} and programl~\cite{programl} library.
elements.id-string-118: Our tokenizer is specifically designed to handle the pre-processing of code data required for a language model.
elements.id-string-119: It includes tokenizers such as the ast-tokenizer.
elements.id-string-120: As a result, \ourwork can accommodate models (such as augAST~\cite{chen2023learning-dataset}) that require AST as input in the pipeline.
elements.id-string-122: Datasets are crucial for any machine learning application.
elements.id-string-123: Within the \ourwork framework, we contribute HPC-specific datasets either by converting existing ones into \face-compatible formats or by creating new ones from scratch.
elements.id-string-124: We have converted three existing datasets to be compatible with \face dataset API: POJ-104~\cite{dataset:poj104}, DRB-ML~\cite{osti_1958879}, and \crawldata~\cite{chen2023learning-dataset}.
elements.id-string-125: POJ-104 is derived from a pedagogical programming open judge (OJ) system that automatically evaluates the validity of submitted source code for specific problems by executing the code.
elements.id-string-126: This dataset is particularly useful for the code similarity task.
elements.id-string-127: The DRB-ML dataset contains 658 C/C++ OpenMP kernels derived from DataRaceBench~\cite{dataset:dataracebench}.
elements.id-string-128: We extended it to have labels indicating if a kernel is parallelizable or not.
elements.id-string-129: The \crawldata dataset is an open-source benchmark composed of data from three resources: code crawled from GitHub, OpenMP benchmarks such as Nas Parallel Benchmarks~\cite{jin1999openmp} and Rodinia~\cite{che2009rodinia}, and synthetic code.
elements.id-string-130: This dataset contains loops with labels indicating whether a loop is parallel and, if parallelizable, the corresponding OpenMP directive associated with the loop.
elements.id-string-131: Furthermore, we have manually created a new OpenMP question answering dataset called OMPQA in order to probe the capabilities of language models in single-turn interactions with users.
elements.id-string-132: Similar to other QA datasets, we include some request-response pairs which are not strictly question-answering pairs.
elements.id-string-133: The categories and examples of questions in the OMPQA dataset can be found in  Table~\ref{tab-omp-qa}.

elements.id-string-141: Language models derive knowledge from training datasets and store this knowledge in internal weights within the model's neural network architecture.
elements.id-string-142: However, incorporating new information into a trained model presents a challenge.
elements.id-string-143: Traditionally, one might fine-tune pre-trained models with their own data for specific tasks, but this approach requires substantial relevant data and can be resource-intensive.
elements.id-string-144: An alternative approach involves integrating new data as context information into a user prompt, but this is constrained by the limited input token lengths of current models.
elements.id-string-145: To address this challenge, \ourwork leverages the LangChain framework~\cite{langchain2023} to easily integrate new data.
elements.id-string-146: LangChain aggregates a wide variety of components to build applications using LLMs.
elements.id-string-147: Particularly, it provides APIs allowing LLM applications to store large amounts of text in semantic databases called vector stores.
elements.id-string-148: The way to integrate new data can be done in two steps.
elements.id-string-149: First, text data is chunked and embedded with an LLM before being saved into a vector store.
elements.id-string-150: Later, user prompts are matched with relevant chunks in the vector store using similarity analysis.
elements.id-string-151: The top-matched chunks are then injected into the original prompts to form a new prompt with relevant context information.
elements.id-string-152: By employing this new prompt, language models can generate answers that incorporate new and relevant user data while still staying within the token length limits.
elements.id-string-154: An easily accessible harness for evaluating different language models on HPC tasks is crucial.
elements.id-string-155: Standard and reproducible results from such evaluations can provide researchers and developers with insightful starting points, helping them select suitable models for their specific needs and identify research opportunities.
elements.id-string-156: In response to this need, we developed an evaluator API in \ourwork.
elements.id-string-157: One challenge we encountered is the lack of standardized metrics for code evaluation.
elements.id-string-158: Unlike natural language tasks, where metrics such as BLEU,
elements.id-string-161: are commonly used, the domain of code lacks such universally accepted measures of quality.
elements.id-string-162: We are adding various LLM metrics such as CodeBLEU~\cite{ren2020codebleu} for code output.
elements.id-string-163: Another challenge is that language models may generate different answers for the same input in different inference runs.
elements.id-string-164: Evaluation should consider consistent sampling settings (such as temperatures) and control over random seeds to improve reproducibility.
elements.id-string-165: Ultimately, many users are interested in seeing leaderboards that showcase mainstream models competing on common HPC tasks.
elements.id-string-166: To satisfy this interest, we create and release a set of test harnesses scripts to enable standard and reproducible evaluation for supported HPC tasks.
elements.id-string-168: In this section, we evaluate the current prototype implementation of LM4HPC through experiments designed to generate leaderboards for three representative tasks: Code Similarity Analysis, Parallelism Detection, and OpenMP Question Answering.
elements.id-string-169: \ourwork utilizes LangChain v0.0.174, \face's transformers v4.29.0 and datasets v2.12.0 as our runtime libraries.
elements.id-string-170: Details of the models and datasets will be discussed in subsequent subsections.
elements.id-string-171: Our experiments were conducted on two machines: 1) a Google Colab VM with a 6-core Xeon processor operating at 2.20GHz, 83.5 GB main memory, 166GB HDD drive, and an NVIDIA A100 GPU with 40 GB memory.
elements.id-string-172: 2) a Dell workstation equipped with a dual Intel Xeon 6238 CPU operating at 2.10GHz, 128 GB main memory, 1TB SSD drive, and an NVIDIA Quadro RTX 6000 GPU with 24GB memory.
elements.id-string-173: The majority of our experiments were run on the Google Colab machine to leverage its superior GPU memory.
elements.id-string-174: However, we encountered difficulties running Cerebras-GPT on the Colab machine and were compelled to use the Dell workstation with larger CPU memory instead.
elements.id-string-176: The code similarity task is designed to measure the syntactic and/or semantic similarity between two code snippets.
elements.id-string-177: Such analysis information can be beneficial in various scenarios such as plagiarism detection, code reuse and refactoring, bug detection and repair, licensing compliance, malware detection, and so on.
elements.id-string-179: Two datasets introduced in Section~\ref{sec-datasets}, POJ-104 and DRB-ML, are loaded through \ourwork's datasets API for this experiment.
elements.id-string-180: For each pair of code snippets in the POJ-104 dataset, we assign a binary similarity label based on their functional labels.
elements.id-string-181: A similarity label of 1 signifies that the snippet pair shares the same functional label and we assign a similarity score of 1.
elements.id-string-183: We have processed the DRB-ML dataset using a similar methodology to generate code pairs and labels.
elements.id-string-184: The main difference is that the similarity ground truth for DRB-ML is derived from its own similarity score table~\cite{chen2022early}, providing a precise and reliable similarity measurement between code snippets in the dataset.
elements.id-string-186: We employ \ourwork's code similarity pipeline to test various models.
elements.id-string-187: The default model for this pipeline is CodeBERT.
elements.id-string-188: We additionally select four models from Table \ref{tab-modelExample} for evaluation: GraphCodeBERT, gpt-3.5-turbo, Dolly 2.0 (12B), and Cerebras-GPT (13B).
elements.id-string-189: We set the maximum token length for the model output to 256.
elements.id-string-190: This limits the verbosity of the model and keeps its responses concise.
elements.id-string-191: Additionally, we set the temperature parameter to 0 when applicable.
elements.id-string-192: For models like Dolly 2.0 that require positive temperature, we set the temperature to be $1\times 10^{-6}$.
elements.id-string-193: This setting ensures that the model's responses are consistent and deterministic, minimizing variability and uncertainty in its output.
elements.id-string-194: Within \ourwork, the approach of processing input code pairs depends on the type of the model employed.
elements.id-string-195: Models like CodeBert and GraphCodeBert are specifically devised and trained on a variety of programming languages.
elements.id-string-196: We directly feed a pair of code snippets to generate a similarity prediction.
elements.id-string-197: On the other hand, large language models like gpt-3.5-turbo, Dolly 2.0, and Cerebras-GPT are evaluated using the following prompt template: ``Code 1: \{...\} Code 2: \{...\}  Determine whether the two code snippets are similar.
elements.id-string-198: If the code snippets are similar, output 1; otherwise, output 0.''.
elements.id-string-200: The Code Similarity Analysis leaderboards generated using the two datasets are shown in Table~\ref{tab:hpctask1}.
elements.id-string-202: Two other models, StarChat-Alpha and Dolly 2.0, also exhibit commendable performance.
elements.id-string-203: Most large language models outperform traditional models (GraphCodeBERT and CodeBERT) that were specifically trained for code analysis.
elements.id-string-204: However, Cerebras-GPT struggled to comprehend the code and mostly returned arbitrary word tokens, indicating a lack of effective code understanding since it is mostly designed for natural language processing.

elements.id-string-212: The parallelism detection task aims to identify parallelism opportunities within a given code snippet.
elements.id-string-213: We utilized two datasets, \crawldata  and DRB-ML introduced in Section~\ref{sec-datasets}, for the experiment.
elements.id-string-214: The \crawldata dataset is specifically designed for parallelism detection.
elements.id-string-215: Its existing labeling scheme allows us to prepare the data for binary classification models.
elements.id-string-216: Similarly, we prepared DRB-ML dataset with a label indicating whether each code snippet is parallelizable using OpenMP or not.
elements.id-string-217: It is worth noting that both datasets have undergone source code pre-processing steps, including comment removal and code snippet extraction.
elements.id-string-218: These steps are common practice~\cite{chen2023learning-dataset} to ensure that code snippets are small enough to be fed into language models with limited input token sequence sizes.
elements.id-string-219: However, the resulting code snippets may lose their context information, such as variable declarations.
elements.id-string-220: This is a serious limitation of language models with limited input sizes when applied to process large source files.
elements.id-string-222: We selected six models to generate parallelism detection leaderboards.
elements.id-string-223: Four of them are introduced in Section~\ref{sec-background}.
elements.id-string-224: They take the code snippets in a prompt template: ``As an OpenMP expert, you will analyze the given code snippet to determine if it can be parallelized.
elements.id-string-227: The other two are augAST~\cite{chen2023learning-dataset} and DeepSCC-based~\cite{harel2023learning}, which are pre-trained models using \crawldata's training dataset.
elements.id-string-228: We fed code snippets to these two models to directly obtain predicted labels.
elements.id-string-230: The highest F1 score reaches 93.9, indicating that LMs can be very effective for detecting parallelism.

elements.id-string-268: To enhance the capacity of large language models (LLMs) in accurately responding to OpenMP queries, we integrate the official OpenMP documentation into our process.
elements.id-string-269: We employ LangChain, a mechanism designed to efficiently store and retrieve language model embeddings, enabling us to accommodate large volumes of new data.
elements.id-string-270: To assess the efficacy of using LangChain to incorporate additional user data, we leverage its API to create a vector store.
elements.id-string-271: This vector store holds embeddings of text chunks derived from the OpenMP API Specification v5.2 (669 pages) and the OpenMP Application Programming Interface Examples v5.2.1 (575 pages).
elements.id-string-272: We then select two LangChain-supported models, GPT-3.5 and Dolly 2.0, to utilize the vector store as an additional resource for answering queries, thereby demonstrating the practical utility of our approach.
elements.id-string-273: The results indicate slight improvements in both the BLEU and ROUGE-L F1 scores, increasing from 0.139 to 0.147 and from 0.257 to 0.259, respectively.
elements.id-string-274: However, there are mixed results for recall and precision metrics.
elements.id-string-275: gpt-3.5-turbo has a better recall, 0.446, compared to 0.347 of the Langchain approach.
elements.id-string-276: Further, we examine the effectiveness of the LangChain approach across different question categories.
elements.id-string-277: When addressing `Basic' questions, the BLEU scores rise by 20.7\% and 9.8\% for gpt-3.5-turbo and Dolly 2.0, respectively.
elements.id-string-278: Additionally, we assess the LangChain performance using the CodeBLEU metric\cite{ren2020codebleu} for the `Examples' category, observing a score increase of 6.1\% and 12.2\% for gpt-3.5-turbo and Dolly 2.0, respectively.
elements.id-string-279: These observations indicate that augmenting LLMs with documentation via LangChain improves performance for `Basic' and `Examples' categories.
elements.id-string-280: However, for `Compilers' and `Benchmarks' categories, the performance of gpt-3.5-turbo and Dolly 2.0 diminishes when utilizing LangChain, recording an average BLEU score drop of 8.0\% and 7.9\%, respectively.
elements.id-string-281: This drop is likely because our documentation does not include information relevant to compiler and benchmark topics.

elements.id-string-289: PyTorch and TensorFlow are the most popular frameworks, backed by Meta AI and Google, respectively.

elements.id-string-291: \face is best known for its \texttt{Transformers} library, which exposes a collection of Python APIs to leverage state-of-the-art deep learning architectures for NLP tasks.
elements.id-string-292: With the goal to simplify end-to-end NLP tasks, \face \texttt{Transformers} offers a pipeline that performs all pre- and post-processing steps on the given input text data.
elements.id-string-293: The overall process of the model inference is encapsulated within these pipelines.
elements.id-string-294: With the pipeline, users only need to provide the input texts and the model for the task.

elements.id-string-296: There were various research works and developments to improve the ML ecosystem to be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reproducible (FAIR).
elements.id-string-297: These existing frameworks aim to make the models, datasets, or both FAIR.
elements.id-string-298: Among these frameworks, HPCFAIR~\cite{verma2021hpcfair} focuses on providing support for model interoperability, search capabilities for datasets and models, and seamless integration into HPC workflows.
elements.id-string-299: The work in \cite{yu2022seamless} extended this work to include support for interoperability across different framework implementations using ONNX and provision to retrain a model with transfer learning.
elements.id-string-300: However, HPCFAIR framework relies on users to handle data pre- and post-processing.
elements.id-string-301: In comparison, LM4HPC is equipped to manage data processing within the pipeline design and generate leaderboards for supported HPC tasks.

elements.id-string-311: In this paper, we presented our efforts to facilitate the application of language models for tasks specific to High-Performance Computing.
elements.id-string-312: We have developed the LM4HPC framework to encompass and expose relevant machine learning components via corresponding APIs.
elements.id-string-313: Our experimental findings suggest that GPT-3 performs competitively, despite not being specifically designed for HPC tasks.
elements.id-string-314: However, there is significant room for improvement in answering OpenMP questions.
elements.id-string-315: Furthermore, the input size limitation of language models adds complexity to certain tasks, such as parallelism detection.
elements.id-string-316: Finally, an obstacle to advancing the application of language models for HPC tasks is the absence of HPC-specific training and evaluation datasets.
elements.id-string-317: Looking ahead, our future work will explore automated approaches to generating HPC-specific datasets.
elements.id-string-318: We intend to enhance LM4HPC's capabilities to support the fine-tuning of models for HPC-related tasks, including those related to the Message Passing Interface (MPI), and to provide performance analysis and optimization suggestions.
